River surface.observation: The water combines extra pictures of the scene with moving surface detail. It looks rippled without simulating every moving drop of water.

Shallow river.observation: Surface detail changes how light appears to hit the water. The shallow bank helps show where the water meets the land.

Bank and shallows.observation: The riverbank and riverbed use the same path as the water. Their edges must agree so the river does not leave holes or spill onto dry ground.

Submerged detail.observation: A separate picture of the scene supplies what appears below the surface. Depth checks help keep objects in front of the river from appearing underwater.

Curved roof.observation: A 2D outline is extended along the carriage to make the rounded roof. It is real shape, so its outline stays curved from different camera angles.

Wheel area.observation: Wheels and axles are built from cylinder shapes. During a ride, their turn angle comes from how far the train has travelled. This photo shows the parts; the experiment below explains the movement.

Door leaves.observation: Each sliding door moves inside its carriage group. The carriage can follow the track while the door separately opens or closes.

Painted body.observation: The same body shape can look like painted metal or another surface by changing its material settings.

Window strip.observation: The window material lets the carriage interior show through. Reflected light and the window frame help make the glass visible.

Window frames.observation: Frames, glass and body panels sit at different depths. That separation helps the game decide which surface should appear in front.

Cream/red boundary.observation: These colored panels meet at their edges instead of covering exactly the same surface. That avoids flicker when the camera moves.

Station lettering.observation: The letters are drawn into an image and placed on a flat sign. The game does not need a separate 3D shape for every letter.

Diagonal steel members.observation: Each beam needs a length and a direction. The builder points a simple shape between two endpoints instead of placing every corner by hand.

Distant track.observation: The rails look closer together farther away. That is perspective: the camera makes distant objects occupy fewer pixels.

Near track.observation: Nearby sleepers occupy more of the picture. The camera view angle changes how wide and deep the track feels.

Broadleaf crowns.observation: Many trees reuse the same source shapes. Their positions, sizes and colors vary, so the hill does not look like identical copies in a row.

Conifers.observation: Repeated cone-like layers make these trees. The game can draw matching shapes together to reduce repeated drawing instructions.

Rocks.observation: These rocks can share a source shape. Rotating and resizing the copies gives each a different appearance.

Canopy.observation: Code on the graphics processor moves the leaf points to suggest wind. The upper branches move more than the base. A still image shows the affected shape; the experiment explains the motion.

Trunk bases.observation: The bottom of each tree stays steadier than its crown. Otherwise the whole tree would slide or bend away from the ground.

Foreground trees.observation: Nearby trees remain visible. Skipping distant objects saves drawing work, but their data may still be stored in memory.

Falling rain.observation: Thin moving lines make the rain streaks. The buildings stay in place while the game updates the positions of those lines.

Distant skyline.observation: Fog reduces contrast in the distance. It makes faraway scenery fade toward the sky color.

Departure feedback.label: Station destination sign
Departure feedback.observation: The destination board helps the player identify the stop. Whether departure is allowed comes from the driving and station rules; this still image does not show a live clearance.
